en: *Amitābha ('Od dpag med)* — *Śrīkṛṣṇavajrapādadohākoṣaṭīkā* (*Dpal nag po rdo rje zhabs kyi do ha mdzod kyi rgya cher 'grel pa*). Toh. no. 2302. Dergé Tanjur, vol. ZHI, folios 230r.6–242v.7. Although no translator is mentioned here, it appears to have been translated by Vairocanavajra. This is a commentary on the text immediately preceding it. [Add the remainder of the Tibetan text later].

In the language of India: *Śrīkṛṣṇavajrapādadohākośaṭīkā*. In the language of Tibet: *Dpal nag po rdo rje zhabs kyi do ha mdzod kyi rgya cher ’grel pa* (The Extensive Commentary on the Treasury of Dohās by the Glorious Vajrapāda). Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva!
May the honey-sweet flowers of Kṛṣṇa’s words, sprinkled upon the mud of the ocean of saṃsāra by the pure waters of mantra, be victorious for the sake of the world!

May the lotus born from the ocean of the Mantra system— an ocean filled with the stainless waters of saṃsāra— the flower whose fragrance is the nectar for the benefit of beings, Caryāvratī Kṛṣṇa, be ever victorious!
*By Viduṣāmṛtavajra, at the request of his excellent disciple.*
The words composed by Caryāpāda are analyzed individually and separately.
At the request of my own disciple, the wise Vajra of Immeasurable Conduct shall provide a detailed analysis of the words and meaning of the *Dohākośa*.

*Note: Amitavajra says that here, those who are renowned for their pride—thinking with the conceit "We are knowers of reality" because of their mundane false knowledge, and thinking "We know suchness" through their arrogance—they carry the burden of pride, imagining themselves to be experts in reality, saying "We are knowers of reality. Having observed them, Ācārya Caryāvajra, his heart stilled by the weight of compassion, spoke the teaching on the reality of the principles of Mantra as they truly are, in the common vernacular, in order to shatter [their delusions] within and for the benefit of all people.* As for the phrase "the reality of Mantra as it truly is": [this refers to the following].

Having observed those worldly people who, out of deliberate pride, think, "By means of this very false cognition itself, I am one whose nature is skilled in the ultimate meaning," and who consequently boast, "I am one who realizes reality (*tattva*"); [the author proceeds as follows].

With a mind moistened by the burden of compassion and desiring to destroy all of his pride, in order to demonstrate the reality (*tattva*) according to the system of mantras as it truly is, he spoke the words beginning with "The worldly person acts with pride" and so forth, thinking: "For the common benefit of all living beings, I, the master of speech, Cakrapāṇivajra, am skilled in the supreme meaning."
I carry the pride that "I am skilled in the ultimate truth," even though among ten million [of us], there might be but one who is absorbed in the Stainless One (Nirañjana). (1)

"Loaha gavva samuvvahaï" and so forth. People carry pride. What is this pride? It says: "I am an expert in the ultimate reality. And in order to demonstrate that this [pride] should not be employed even when it occurs, he says: "Koḍiha majjham" and so forth. If one should exist in the midst of millions of yogis; "nirañjana" means the Sahaja-body (sahajakāya), because in it the "añjanas"—the afflictions such as passion and aversion—are absent. One whose mind is dissolved and immersed therein is "nirañjanalīna," a lord of yogis, and the sense is that he is like me.

If one asks what it is that worldly people take pride in, it is said: "I am skilled in the ultimate meaning. This is a teaching on the extent of all that exists, rather than a detailed classification. To demonstrate this, it says: "There may be but one among ten million," and so forth; that is to say, if there were even one existing among ten million.

"Free from dust" (viraja) means being separated here from the afflictions such as passion and so forth; it is the innate body (sahajakāya). To have "entered into that" means the mind has entered with certainty into that, i.e., to have entered into the dustless state. The thought is: "I am such a lord of yogins."
Having refuted those who are arrogant due to false knowledge, he speaks with reference to those "wise" ones who, possessing the wisdom of worldly truth,
harbor the conceit that they understand the ultimate truth:
"The wise carry their pride through the authority of the Āgamas, the Vedas, and the Purāṇas."
Just as ripe sirīphala fruits fall and roll outside [the tree]. || 2 ||

"Those who know the scriptures," and so forth. By means of knowledge of the scriptures and the like, the learned carry pride—that is, conceit regarding the knowledge of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Being such as they are, in what [object], like what, and doing what? He says: "In the ripe *śrīphala* fruit," and so forth. In a ripe *śrīphala* fruit, there are bees (*alayaḥ*, *bhramarāḥ*). Just as they hover on the outside, so too, because their vision is preoccupied with and attached to external mantras, mudrās, and the like, they do not perceive the nectar of the profound reality (*tattva*); this is the meaning. And thus it is said in the *Caturdevīparipṛcchā-yogatantra*:
Of the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dharma of the Great Sage,
all those who do not know the true reality indeed find them to be fruitless.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Even by means of ancient scripture and reasoning," it is said that for those scholars who possess knowledge of scripture and so forth, to act with pride is to manifest the pride of thinking they have realized the ultimate truth. To address the question of what such individuals do and how they act, [the text] states: "Like bees toward a ripened fruit," and so on.

It is said: "The happy ones wander and circulate like bees. Here, "bees" refers to honey. "Others" refers to those who wander and circulate from the outside, just as they are. Likewise, they are bound by external mantras, mudrās, and so forth, because they are intensely attached to such views. As for the meaning of the profound reality (*tattva*):

This means that [the teachings] are not the nectar for those of inferior lineage. Accordingly, it is said in the *Caturdevīparipṛcchā*, a Mahāyoga Tantra: "The great Sage’s aggregates of Dharma consist of eighty-four thousand; yet for whoever does not know reality, all of them are fruitless."

If this is so, then how is it that the form of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is directly realized? It is said in reply: even the form of conceptual proliferation—the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—arises from the very beginning from non-proliferated innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*). That very form of proliferation, being produced from that [gnosis], serves as the sign for its realization. Thus it has been said: "By means of conceptual proliferations, one is made free from conceptual proliferation."

If that is so, one might ask: how can the forms of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) be produced in reality? It should be stated that even the forms of conceptual proliferation—the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-fields (*āyatana*), and so forth—arise from that very same non-proliferated innate primordial wisdom (*sahaja-jñāna*). These forms of proliferation emerge from that itself; and for the sake of demonstrating this, it is said as follows:
It is said: "By means of proliferation, one should bring about the non-proliferated."

Therefore, demonstrating how the world arises from such a body that is innate and possesses the forms of woman, man, and neuter, he says: "From that very *evaṃ*, from the syllable of the innate body, [he speaks] in order to show how the world arises."
Adorned with bodhicitta, he is praised by those who are unshakeable;
O daughter of the lotus, he is seen by means of one's own body in its natural state. || 3 ||

"Bohici" and so forth: adorned with the dust of the *bodhicitta*. "Embraced by Akṣobhya. "The void, the extreme void, and the great void. "Light, the appearance of light, and the attainment of light. "Mind, mental factors, and ignorance. [Female, male, and neuter. "Night, day, and twilight. "The *nirmāṇakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *dharmakāya*. "Body, speech, and mind," which are the obstructors of water and vapor. "Invoking, dismissing, and retaining. The syllables "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ."

The openings that pierce the upper and lower vital points (*marmans*) are the gates. These include the principles of the self (*ātmatattva*), the mantra (*mantratattva*), and the maṇḍala (*maṇḍalatattva*); the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; the moon, sun, and Rāhu; and arising, abiding, and dissolution—such things as these. The "dust" (*rajas*) of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is expressed by the word Akṣobhya.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Bodhicitta and so forth," it is said: "Embraced by the body of Akṣobhya through bodhicitta and the [subtle] particles. These refer to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), extreme emptiness (*atiśūnyatā*), and great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*); to appearance (*āloka*), the increase of appearance (*ālokābhāsa*), and the attainment of appearance (*ālokopalabdhi*); and to mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitta*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Woman, man, and hermaphrodite; day, night, and the intermediate period; the nirmāṇakāya, saṃbhogakāya, and dharmakāya; body, speech, and mind; vapor, steam, and complete binding; inviting, requesting to depart, and entering; and the syllables OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ.

"The gates of below, above, and across; the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), the reality of mantra (*mantratattva*), and the reality of the mandala (*maṇḍalatattva*); the essence (*sattva*), the dust (*rajas*), and the darkness (*tamas*); the moon, the sun, and Rāhu; birth, abiding, and destruction"—these and so forth are expressed by the terms "bodhicitta," "dust," and "Akṣobhya."

He asks, "Where has this been seen? and says: "The lotus-seed," and so forth. *Puṣkara* is the body-lotus; its *bīja* (seed) is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which is pure and stainless because of its luminosity. That very [nature] is the Sahajakāya. Where has this been seen or understood? [... This is the meaning: the Blessed One, the King of Body, Speech, and Mind, abided in the realm of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyadhātu*). The world itself is of the form of the syllable *Evaṃ*. [The reading is *bījasvabhāvam*; the variant is *śuddhanirmalam*.]

Regarding the phrase "In this way, where is it seen? and so forth, it is said: "The naturally pure innate [nature] is seen within the body, like the nature of a lotus seed. Here, the lotus-body itself is the "lotus"; its seed is the "nature. It is "pure" because it is stainless and naturally luminous; that very [purity] is the innate body (*sahaja-kāya*).

Thinking, "Where is this seen and realized? it is seen within one's own body; the meaning of this is that the Bhagavān arises from body, speech, and mind. He has entered the realm of universal emptiness and is the very essence of the syllable *E-Vaṃ*.
And so it is said in the *Ādibuddhatantra*:
"The body consists of two drops: the semen (*śukra*) and the emission of speech (*vāgvisarga*), which is the dust (*rajas*) and the sun (*ravi*).
This very syllable *Evaṃ* is Rāhu in the form of the fire of time (*kālāgni*), the sole seed of the entire world."

Thus, it is said in the *Ādibuddhatantra*: "The *bindu* of the body is the moon and the bodhicitta; speech is the *visarga*, the dust, and the sun. This mind, which is the fire of the *rāhu*-time, is the single seed-syllable *ĀḤ* and *VAṂ* for all wandering beings.
Therefore, he says:
"The circle of *ḍākinīs* arises, abides, dissolves, and is pacified."
Therefore, from that single syllable *vaṃ*, the manifold universe arises in many forms.

For this very reason, it is said that the wheel of ḍākinīs consists of arising, abiding, dissolving, and utter pacification. Therefore, from the syllables *ae* and *waṃ*, the manifold world of beings emerges.

But from a single lump of clay, only one effect characterized as a jar produced by the transformation of that lump arises. How then is it that from a single [cause] there arises a world of manifold forms, manifold shapes, and manifold locations, arising incessantly and without end?

Just as from a single lump of clay there arises a single fruit characterized as a jar made from that clay, how is it that from that one [lump] there arise various forms, shapes, and directions, existing continuously and without end?
It is said: There is no fault at all—just as knowledge comes from a teacher, or as a lamp arises from a lamp.
The counter-seal of a seal is like a face reflected from a face in a mirror.
Just as an echo arises from a sound, or fire from a sun-crystal,
or as the sun is not produced without the sun, so too the ringing in the ears arises from eating sour food.
Never, anywhere, do any entities whatsoever exist that have arisen from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause.
The white [semen] of the father and the red [blood] of the mother, as well as the pair of prāṇa and apāna,
conjoined with the mind-vajra, are the causes for the arising of the body.
Amitābha and Ratnadhṛk are, respectively, the out-breath and the in-breath;
they are the body, speech, mind, and passion of the Mind-Vajra-holder.
From semen the moon is produced; from blood arises the sun;
from the prāṇa comes the manifestation of Rāhu, and from the apāna, that of Kālāgni.
From semen arises the formation of the channels; from semen arises the production of bone. From the menstrual flow (rajas) arises the production of blood; from blood arises the production of flesh.
From flesh and skin, birth arises; marrow exists within the marrow and bones.
From the moon, water is produced; from the production of fire, blood arises.
The production of the prāṇa is from Rāhu, and that of the apāna is said to be from Agni;
the tongue and the uvula of all embodied beings are produced by Śukra.
The left and right eyes were produced from *rajas*,
and likewise, the two nostrils were surely produced by *prāṇa*.
The two ear-cavities are likewise produced from the void (śūnya) alone; the pair of testicles arises from the downward-breath (apāna), and thus their manifestation occurs therein.

This shall now be explained: Just as it is known from preceptors, as a lamp [is known] from a lamp, as a seal [is known] from a seal, as a face [is known] from a mirror, as an echo arises from a sound, as fire arises from a fire-crystal, as fire [is known] from the sun’s form at midday, and as [taste is known] when one who has not eaten sour food salivates—[it is] neither from itself nor from another.

Neither from both, nor without a cause, is there ever the arising of any entity whatsoever. Semen and blood from the father and mother, as well as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the downward-clearing wind (*apāna*), and the vajra of the mind, are the causes that produce the body. Amitābha, Ratnasambhava, and Apāna, in their respective order, are the passion of body, speech, and mind.

The faces are the vajra of the mind; from semen arises the moon, and from blood arises the sun, which is existence (*bhava*). From the vital breath (*prāṇa*) arises *rāhu*. From the downward-clearing wind (*apāna*) arises the fire of time (*kāla-vahni*). From semen arise the channels (*nāḍī*); from semen arise the bones. From the dust (*rajas*) blood arises, and from flesh the skin is born; from the bones the marrow arises.

From the moon arises the water-born [semen]; from the blood, fire comes into being. From Rāhu, life-force is born; from the fire of time, apāna arises. Through exertion, the mind comes into being. For all embodied beings, the uvula and the tongue arise from the semen; and from the dust [of the female element], the two eyes arise on the right and left.

Likewise, the two nostrils arise definitively from blood; likewise, the two ear canals arise from emptiness itself. Likewise, the three lower apertures arise perfectly from the downward-clearing wind (apāna); likewise, the two breasts arise perfectly from rāhu. Likewise, the two testicles arise thoroughly from the downward-clearing wind.
In this manner, by this sequence, the lotus-born [Brahmā] is produced.

And then, demonstrating the collection of conditions for its production through the sequence of the conventional and the ultimate, he says: "Thus, since the lotus of the body arises here in this sequence, therefore, in order to demonstrate the collection of conditions for its arising by way of the conventional and ultimate sequences— "
The sky, water, nectar, and mud are conceived as being devoid of root;
even the pride of one who has shaken off the root and the stalk becomes [rootless]. 4.

"Sky-water," and so forth. The sky is Akṣobhya; he is described as water because of his extreme purity. And it is said: "Space is the *amṛtabindu*. "Amiāha-pāṃka" means Amitābha, the bodhicitta adorned with *rajas*; that itself is the mud (*paṅka*). Having done what? Having made the root, which is the primary cause. That very thing is manifested as great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

This is the meaning: even a small seed, when combined with water and mud, produces sprouts, stalks, and so forth; likewise, this seed of the *dharmadhātu*, having space as its water and the *bodhicitta* as its cause, brings forth that Blessed One—the unstruck (*anāhata*) lotus in the form of existence—through the sequence of stalk, petal, and stem. Thus he says: "The *avadhūtī* made the root-stalk," and so on.
Because she shakes away (*dhūta*) evil (*avaṃ*), destroying it by means of her nature of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), she is the *avadhūtī*, the first [channel].

Regarding the passage beginning with "the water of space" and so forth: "space" refers to Akṣobhya; he is symbolized as water because he is utterly pure in this way. As it is said: "The drops of nectar of space. Regarding "the mud of Amitābha": "Amitābha" refers to the bodhicitta.

It should be understood as "adorned with dust. From that same [text]: "The abandonment of the mud's roots" indicates the intermediate state (*madhyama-tattva*). The meaning of this is also found elsewhere: just as sprouts, stalks, and so forth arise when seeds, water, and mud are assembled, so too [arise] the *dharmadhātu* as the seed and space as the water.

That very indestructible form of the Blessed One, which arises from the cause of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), becomes fully perfected through the sequence of stem, branches, and leaves, having the nature of a lotus flower. Regarding this, it is said: "That itself, having abandoned evil, together with its root and trunk," and so forth. Here, "abandoning" refers to the destruction of the faults of sin.
Because it is luminosity itself, it is called "Abandoning Sin" (*Pāpaha*), as it destroys [sin] by this means; it has the nature of the first vowel.
And likewise, in the *Ādibuddhatantra*:
"That which is the nature of the primordial vowel is designated as 'intellect' (dhī) by the Buddhas. Thus it is said.

That whose root and primary stalk are made by the *avadhūtī* alone is called "the one with the *avadhūtī* as its root-stalk. What is this? It is the seed-syllable *haṃ*, which is designated as the "I-maker" (*ahaṃkāra*) according to the systems of other [schools]. That very [syllable] is the *anāhata*. It is "after *kṣa*" (i.e., ending in the letter *kṣa*). It is the fourth of the sibilants (*ūṣman*). It is the syllable of Vajrānaṅga. All forms consisting of the combination of short, long, and protracted [vowels] are the single seed of bliss, situated within the full moon-maṇḍala.

It is that which abandons evil and makes the primary root its trunk. If one asks what it is that abandons evil and makes the primary root its trunk, it is said to be the generation of the syllable *HAṂ*. It is described as the seed of faith taught by another; it is that very [syllable] which is the invincible state beyond [the ordinary], the manner of the mouth, namely *HAṂ*.

This is the syllable of Acala-vajra. It is short and long; it is said to abide within the full orb of the moon, which is the essence of the condensed extremely long [vowel] and the essence of all bliss condensed into one.
And so it is said in the Śrīsampuṭa:
"That which arises from vowels and consonants, consisting of the thirty-two aspects of the mind of awakening,
situated in the center of the lotus— that is called the lunar mandala."
That which is situated in the center of the head is declared to be the brain;
in its center, however, is the syllable *haṃ*, the unstruck (*anāhata*) sound in the form of a point (*bindu*).
That is the root of all beings, both the stable and those of a mobile nature;
it is stable in the form of a seed, manifest through its unmanifest form.
From that, the form of all embodied beings arose at the very beginning;
it flows in the form of nectar, remaining established day and night.
By that very sound which brings satisfaction to the fire, the mandala becomes completely full; of this there is no doubt.
That very essence is called "maṇḍa," the supreme quintessence of all things;
because it grasps (gṛhṇāti) and takes (lāti) that, the body is considered a "maṇḍala."

Thus, it is said in the *Śrī-Sampuṭatilaka*: "From the vowels and consonants, the thirty-two syllables of bodhicitta arise. This is called the mantra that realizes the lotus maṇḍala, as well as the tantra and the maṇḍala itself. That which is said to reside in the center of the brain of living beings—within its center is the syllable HAṂ, the indestructible nature of the bindu."

That is the cause that gives rise to all sentient beings, both the stable and the moving; it abides as the very nature of its seed through forms that are manifest and unmanifest. From it, the form of every embodied being without exception first arises. By way of dripping nectar, it remains throughout day and night; by way of entering downward, it remains as a blazing fire.

There is no doubt that this will become a complete maṇḍala; because it is the supreme essence of all things, it is called "reality" (tattva) and "maṇḍala. By taking up and grasping that reality, the body itself is asserted to be the maṇḍala.

Regarding the phrase *vi jāia*: here, the word *vi* is a Prakrit syntactic ornament (*vākyālaṃkāra*). *Jāia* means "born" (*jātaḥ*). It refers to the *haṃkāra* (the sound *haṃ*) characterized as previously described.

Regarding the phrase "arising in various ways" (*rnam par skyes par 'gyur ba*): here, "various ways" (*rnam pa*) refers to the ornamentation of ordinary speech; "arising" (*skyes pa*) refers to that which emerges from the syllable *haṃ* as previously described.

Now, if the *avadhūtī* has been made the central stalk (*mūlanālī*), one might ask: "What are the lotus-stalks, leaves, and so forth? To this he says: *Lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī are the stalks; iḍā and piṅgalā are the branches and leaves.*
In the great blissful abode, there is a fourfold row of lotus petals with four stalks standing firm. || 5 ||

By the word *lalanā*, the *ali* (vowel), which is wisdom (*prajñā*) and the moon, is designated. By its nature as the left nostril, the *lalanā* is situated as the channel through which the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) flows. By the word *rasanā*, the *kāli* (consonant), which is means (*upāya*) and the sun, is denoted. By its nature as the right nostril, the *rasanā* is situated as the channel through which the vital breath flows. According to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), the five mandalas—consisting of consciousness (*vijñāna*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), perception (*saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*), and form (*rūpa*)—belong to the *lalanā*.

In the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), the [channels] of the tongue consist of the natures of earth, water, fire, air, and space. Thus, during the flow of the uneven and even [breaths] through the revolution of the twelve zodiacal signs (*dvādaśalagna*), the *lalanā* and *rasanā* experience thirty mandalas each. Regarding the terms *lalanā-rasanā* or simply *ṣaṇḍa ṭhia*, it is for this reason that two *ṣaṇḍas* are situated. As it is said: "The *lalanā* exists by nature as wisdom (*prajñā*), while the *rasanā* is established as means (*upāya*); but the *avadhūtī* in the middle region is devoid of both the grasped and the grasper."

That which was stated as "ava" refers to the four-petaled [lotus] whose nature is the four voids (*catuḥśūnya*). "Caü muṇāla" means situated upon four lotus stalks (*muṇāla*), having the nature of the four channels (*nāḍī*). Where? He says: in the abode of great bliss (*mahāsukhāvāsa*). The abode of great bliss is that which consists of the four joys (*caturānanda*) and has the essence of the four voids; it is called the "abode of great bliss" because great bliss dwells therein—the *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus, which is the dwelling place of the all-void (*sarvaśūnya*). It is the gathering place (*melāpaka*) of the network of *ḍākas* and *ḍākinīs*, meaning the summit of Mount Meru known as Jālandhara.
Taking the lotus flower whose seed-syllable is "Evaṃ," the hero of the gods, in the form of a bee, drinks its nectar. (6)

"Taking the seed-syllable *evaṃ*": having taken the seed-syllable *evaṃ*, which possesses the characteristics already described, that seed-syllable becomes the interior (*garbha*) of the blossoming *anāhata-lotus*. This is the meaning: whatever tree or other plant is produced from a particular seed, the flower of that tree also contains that very same seed within its interior. Here, the flower of the lotus produced from the syllable *evaṃ* likewise has the syllable *evaṃ* as its interior. "In the form of a honey-bee," and so forth.

The "bee" (madhukara) is the mind-vajra; he "smells" (jighrati), that is, perceives its own form (svarūpa). "Suratavīra" means the union in pairs (dvandvayoga) of wisdom and means. Therein, he is a "hero" (vīra) because, by means of the nature of uninterrupted great passion (mahārāga), he destroys detachment (virāga). He is that very Blessed One, the Unstruck Sound (nāhata); "he smells" (jiṃghaï) means he perceives. "Nectar" (makaranda) refers to the essence of the flower. The meaning is that through his heroism in sexual union (suratavīratā), he experiences the bliss of unchanging great passion. Such is the Blessed One, whose form is the syllable EṂ.
Anticipating the question, "How is he born as consisting of the five great elements accompanied by outflows (sāsrava)? he says:
"The five great elements, having taken up the seed, unite through a combination; thus earth, water, fire, wind, and space are joined together. (7)

"The five great elements (mahābhūta), having taken the seed-syllable," and so forth. The "great elements" are the pentad beginning with earth. Having taken the "seed" which is the syllable *EṂ*, that which is born or produced arises through the totality [of conditions], by means of the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*. Demonstrating that very point, he says: "Solid is earth," and so forth. Because of its hardness, the earth element is solid; because of its fluidity, the water element; because of its heat, the fire element; because of its movement, the wind element; and because of its nature as bliss (*sukha*), the space element.
In this place, which is as pleasant as the breeze from the sky and filled with the five [senses], all the gods and demons have come; yet, O friend, this very thing is empty.
"Filled with the five" means that the *bodhicitta* is filled with, that is, joined with, these five elements (*pañcabhūta*). And so it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:

"Why is there a physical aggregate (*bhautikaskandha*)? The Blessed One replied: "By the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, through the quality of hardness arising from contact, earth is produced therein."
And from the water element, there is the arising in the form of the fluid bodhicitta.
"Fire is produced from friction; wind is proclaimed [to arise] from movement;
bliss and the space-element are enveloped by these five.

For this very reason, it says: "Complete with the five. It is filled and joined together by these five. "The origin of all gods and asuras," and so forth. This means the cause of the arising of all humans and non-humans, gods and asuras. "Ehu" (this) refers to this very thing. This is the meaning.
"The four principles beginning with earth are the four voids;
these eight categories should be known as the causes of destruction and origination.
Thus, from the luminous [void] comes the great void, and from that, the arising of skillful means.
From that, wisdom arises; from that, the wind is produced.
From wind arises fire, and from fire arises water;
from water the earth is born—this is the origin of all beings.
The earth element dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire;
fire dissolves into the subtle element; and wind dissolves into the mind.

"The mind (*citta*) dissolves into the mental factors (*caitasika*), and the mental factors dissolve into ignorance (*avidyā*); that [ignorance] too goes into the luminous (*prabhāsvara*). This is cessation within the three worlds.

Thus it is said: "Foolish one! This is emptiness," and so forth. Because this is not outside of the Vehicle (Yāna), the word *baḍha* is a vocative particle: "O fool, you who do not know the reality of the Mantra system! "This very thing is emptiness" means that the all-empty is the luminosity; therefore, there is no other reality of emptiness.

Thus it was said by him: "This very Blessed One, the Vajra of Great Bliss whose single nature is both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa, having himself manifested the lotus of his own body, remains intent upon extracting the unstruck floral nectar [of bliss] in the form of the bee of the mind, without interruption. And likewise in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"He himself is the creator, he himself is the destroyer; he himself is the king, he himself is the lord."

Having thus determined the nature of the goal (*sādhya*), one must now consider the means (*sādhana*). First of all, for the abandonment of the enjoyment of sense objects, or even for attachment to sense objects, this is not the means, because he is established in neither the Śrāvaka nor the Pāramitā systems. Since it has been shown that the perfect awakening to great passion (*mahārāga*) and so forth occurs precisely through unfeigned non-attachment to all sense objects, the splendor of the bliss of sense objects itself is his means. And so Saraha says: "Some abandon sense objects; some take sense objects as their foundation; but some bulls among men bring about awakening by means of sense objects alone."

"By whatever means the world is bound, by those very same means one should release that bondage."
The world is deluded; lacking the knowledge of reality, it does not attain perfection.
The world is bound by passion and is liberated by passion alone;
this inverted conception has indeed not been understood by the followers of the Buddha and other outsiders.

If this is so, then all living beings, being attached to sense objects, should likewise attain the perfect awakening of great passion (*mahārāgābhisaṃbodhi*). For it is not the case that the uninterrupted bliss of great passion is obtained merely by the enjoyment of sense objects; such is the sequence. Rather, it is attained through that very means [of practice]; for without the means, and without the syllable-form of the sense objects, there is no realization of the bliss of great passion due to the lack of thorough knowledge of the three appearances (*ābhāsa-traya*). And thus it is said in the *Jñānavajrasamuccayamahāyogatantra*:

He who is attached solely to the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*, making that his ultimate goal, does not attain the awakening of great passion (*mahārāga*). Rather, when he takes up mere pleasure and remains on the stage of a beginner through mere resolute conviction, he remains a learner (*śaikṣa*). But he who, through the bliss of the union of the *vajra* and the *padma*, knows the natural radiance, the true quality, and the characteristic, enters into the bliss of great passion.
And so it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"By whatever terrible deeds sentient beings are bound..."
But by that very same means, together with its method, they are liberated from the bonds of existence.

But is it not the case that even that which possesses a means is merely a cause for the pleasure of sense objects, whereas great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is without a cause (*nirnimitta*); how then can it be so? Indeed, that very pleasure which possesses a cause becomes causeless through the instruction of a true guru. Thus said the venerable Saraha: "That which is this pleasure possessing a cause, that very same [pleasure], when freed from the great cause, [becomes] devoid of causes."
Knowledge is the self-arisen form, great bliss, and empty of conceptual construction.
The bliss with signs;
the self-arisen form of gnosis. (Note: Although attributed to Saraha, the source of this citation remains unidentified.)
Therefore, the enjoyment of the object together with the means is itself the means for achieving the perfect awakening of great passion.
For that very [consciousness] indeed—
taking on the measurements of earth, water, fire, wind,
and space— assumes the proportions of the mandala-cakra and the various perceptions.

"Earth, water, fire," and so forth. Earth is the earth-maṇḍala; water is the water-maṇḍala; fire is the fire-maṇḍala; wind is the wind-maṇḍala; and sky is the space-maṇḍala. These very five are illuminated according to the sequence of creation and dissolution, through the distinction of the Moon and the Sun. And thus it is said in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*:
"Space and the others [are worshipped] always on the left as dissolution, while earth and the others are on the right.
Also, in the *Śrī-Samājottara*:
Having expelled the breath, which consists of the five wisdoms and has the nature of the five elements,
one should visualize it in the form of a single mass at the tip of the lotus-nose.
"The great jewel of five colors is known as *prāṇāyāma*.
Having meditated upon one's own mantra in the heart, one should place the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the *bindu*. Thus it is said.
Regarding this, he provides a further explanation in the *Vajrajvālanāgnimahāyogatantra*:

"At the tip of the nose is that which is called the mustard seed (*sarṣapa*), through the visualization of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Within that breath control reside the five rays by virtue of the state of the Buddhas."
And so Vajragarbhapāda says:

"When the space-maṇḍala flows initially through either the left or right nostril, it then flows in the middle. When the wind-maṇḍala flows, it touches the left nostril-passage. When the fire-maṇḍala [flows], it touches the right nostril-passage. When the water-maṇḍala [flows], it is directed upward. When the earth-maṇḍala flows, it touches downward. This is the wheel of the maṇḍalas."

"Taking the intellect (*buddhi*) as the object (*viṣaya*)," it is said. The "object" is the union of the vajra and the lotus. When that exists, the intellect which is the experience of bliss—that is the *jñānamudrā*; that is the blissful "intellect-as-object. Beings attain this; that is the mandala-circle. Know it by its measure in every respect, such that it becomes established in the sixth consciousness, or know it from the [first] step (*pratipad*).
By this, he explains what it is like:
"Waveless, equal, of the nature of the innate, free from all impurities; devoid of sin and merit, there is nothing else—this is clearly stated. (10)

"Waveless, equal, and of the nature of the innate" means: it is "waveless" because it is devoid of invocation and dismissal; it is "equal" because it has transcended the form of the *kumbha* (the ritual vessel); and it is "of the nature of the innate" because its form is that of the *evaṃkāra* exactly as it is. "Free from all impurities" means: it is free from and liberated from all impurities—that is, all sins—which are of the nature of aversion (*virāga*). As it is said in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*: "There is no sin greater than aversion, nor is there any merit greater than bliss.
Therefore, O King, one should always cause the mind to enter into immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*)."

He says that in such great bliss there is no conceit regarding pleasure: "There is neither sin nor merit; there is only one. Sin is the pleasure of detachment (*vairāgya*); merit is the immutable pleasure (*akṣarasukha*). Not even one of these exists therein. And so it is said in the *Śrīsampuṭa*:
"Having abandoned both passion and detachment, he remains as merit (*puṇya*).
"Clearly told by Kāṇhu": this has been clearly stated by Kṛṣṇa, that is, by Vajra. The meaning is that what is told by others is not clear.

Showing that this cannot be known even through self-yoga by those whose knowledge is directed outwardly, he says: "Outside it is differentiated, within it is undifferentiated; it is established in both the void and the non-void.
But between the void and the non-void, O fool, nothing at all is seen. (11)

"Having gone outside," and so forth: having mentally emerged from the external form-circle (*ākāracakra*) and reached the form-circle as emptiness (*śūnyatva*), and having entered the non-empty [circle] within one's own body through the mental construction of yoga and the like, one becomes focused upon that. "In the middle of both the empty and the non-empty"—the meaning is: O fool, in the midst of these two, the empty and the non-empty, no reality whatsoever has been seen or known.
Anticipating the objection that, if this were so, there would be no reality whatsoever therein, he says:
"There is one innate person there, whom Kṛṣṇa clearly recognizes.
Though he reads and hears many scriptures and traditions, the fool knows nothing at all. (12)

"There is only one innate [nature] (*sahaja*)," and so forth. Only the innate is thus supreme; and Kṛṣṇavajra knows that supreme [nature]. Regarding "the treatises and the scriptures" (*śāstrāgama*): the treatises are logic (*tarka*) and so forth, and the scriptures are the *Kriyā*, *Caryā*, and other [tantras]. One may read, hear, contemplate, and practice these various types [of works], yet one knows nothing at all, because they lack the nature of that [innate reality]. The meaning is that one who knows the instruction on the waveless way of mantras (*nistaraṅga-mantranaya*), such as I am, knows the supreme.
Explaining that very instruction through various words, he says:
"It neither comes nor goes;
free from both, it remains motionless."
He says: "Kṛṣṇa’s heart does not break even in any way;
he remains like a wife in a house where the wind is still. (13)

"Now, 'it does not go,' and so forth. By this function of 'going upwards,' there is the cessation of the three paths of the *prāṇa* wind—distinguished as body, speech, and mind—which are the respective natures of the moon, sun, and Rāhu, and of water, fire, and space. Thus, through the cessation of the paths of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* above and below; by the function of 'going downwards,' there is the cessation of the three paths of the *apāna* wind—distinguished as body, speech, and mind—which are the respective natures of the earth, air, and gnosis elements, and which carry feces, urine, and semen."

When the vision of the reflection of gnosis (jñānabimba), previously indicated, has occurred, thereupon the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) is to be undertaken continuously by means of the method of the downward vajra-recitation (vajrajāpa). And so it is said in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*:
"Once the reflection is seen, one should then perform breath control continuously;
[this is done] by blocking the body, speech, and mind within the three channels above and below."
In those which carry the flow of the moon, sun, Rāhu, feces, urine, and semen;
and in those born from the elements of water, fire, space, earth, wind, and consciousness.
The channels of body, speech, and mind— moon, sun, and darkness— are, respectively,
the carriers of feces, urine, and semen, corresponding to the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
The moon-body is the means (upāya), while speech is the sun;
the wisdom-body (prajñākāya), however, is the feces-channel, which carries urine during enjoyment.
Taminī is the mind of skillful means, while Śukravāhinī is that of wisdom;
these two, Taminī and Śukravāhinī, are the upward and downward channels of the mind.
"This sixfold family above and below is indeed the cause of body, speech, and mind;
it exists in all embodied beings through the division of the limbs of wisdom and means.

This being so, he asks how *prāṇāyāma* remains, and says: "Free from the two, it stands motionless," and so forth. Being free from—that is, liberated from—the two types of *prāṇāyāma*, that which is of such a nature remains motionless as the supreme breath of the middle channel. Likewise, in the *Kulikā*:
Heruka is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), the supreme intermediate breath,
endowed with feces, urine, semen, the sun, and the four channels.
And it is said in the *Vyaktabhāvānugatatattvasiddhi*:
"The innate breath, established in its own place, is freed from the web of conceptual construction."
This [state] of empty nature produces an indescribable satisfaction within the heart.

This being so, demonstrating now the great non-emission of the *bodhicitta*, he says: "He speaks; the mind does not break in any way," and so forth. Kṛṣṇācārya speaks: the mind, which is the *bodhicitta*, does not break—that is, it does not falter—in any way whatsoever. This is because, by the cessation of both modes of movement, it has taken the form of the *kālanāḍī* (the channel of time) swallowed whole.

The intended meaning is as follows: "Let not the drop named Śaśadhara fall"—what is to be accomplished for us by this? Rather, where does this *bodhicitta*, which is of a nature that is neither [of the two] and consists of the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) of the intermediate state, abide? Here [it is said]: "It dwells in the house of the wife who holds the motionless wind," and so forth. The "motionless wind" is the central breath; because it has the nature of the *jñānamudrā*, she is the "wife" (*ghariṇī*), and her "house" is bliss—the element of space, the *avadhūtī*. Therein it dwells, it resides.

This is the intended meaning: here, wind has the nature of motion and is supported by the space element (*ākāśadhātu*). Being led away from the space element—which is itself free from coming and going—it dissolves into the innate (*sahaja*) through the process of ascending, together with the three consciousnesses accompanied by the reflection of light. Therefore, it is said that the Blessed One, the Mahāsukha-vajra, whose essence is that [innate], dwells therein. And so it is stated in the *Anuttarasandhi*:
"Light, the manifestation of light, and likewise the attainment of light—the mind is said to be threefold; its support is now described."
Knowledge, having become mixed with the subtle form of the vital air (vāyu),
issues forth through the pathways of the senses and takes hold of objects.
When the wind, joined with the manifestation (ābhāsa), becomes the vehicle,
then all its constituent elements proceed in both orderly and disordered ways.
Wherever the wind may reside, it carries that very nature;
as long as the breath of the wind continues, it does not become motionless.
Thus, he explains how this becomes common to all people:
"In that excellent mountain cave, even the deep [resonance] of his song causes everyone to break through;
even the pure water there dries up if the fire of cosmic destruction (kālāgni) should enter it. (14)
"Varagirikandara," and so forth. *Vara* means the most excellent mountain, which consists of the form of the staff (*daṇḍa*) of the cave (*kandara*). And thus it is said in the *Śrīsampuṭa*:
"The wind, in the form of Bhairambha and shaped like a bow, is situated at the base of the feet;
likewise, fire is situated in the triangle at the region of the three-fold waist."
For Varuṇa, in the form of a circle, resides in the belly;
and the Earth, square on all sides, resides in the heart.
For Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is likewise in the form of a skeleton staff.

Its *kandara* is a cave or hollow. That very place is beyond the range of body, speech, mind, and thought; what does it become? "The entire world perishes," and so forth. The entire world (*jagat*) indeed perishes—that is, trembles—there; above that, it does not extend even to its summit. This is because the mind is unstable due to the conceit of pleasure derived from the union of the two organs (*dvīndriya-kunduru*). Now, by what sign is it known that the world perishes within this? He says: "The pure water there goes to dryness."

Through its stainless manifestation as the form of bliss, and through its conventional manifestation as the liquid of bliss, the stainless Bodhicitta—the knowledge of the reality of the planets—is what withers and falls downward. For Bodhicitta is the very self of the world; when it falls downward, the entire world perishes and dies. And so it is said in the *Ādibuddha*:
"In death for all embodied beings, the lunar nectar goes downward;
The solar dust and Rāhu [go] upward, within consciousness characterized by existence."

Regarding this, he asks "What would happen there? and says: "The fire of time blazes forth. Time is fire; the state of emission (*cyuti*) is characterized by the entry into the first day of the dark fortnight. This is the time of death. And so it is stated in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*:
"Emission gives rise to dispassion (*virāga*); from dispassion arises suffering;
from suffering comes the depletion of the elements for men; and from that depletion, death is produced."
From death comes rebirth for them, and from that, old age, death, and passing away once more;
thus arises the birth of sentient beings, and existence does not occur otherwise.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid the passion for emission,
by which the yogi attains imperishable bliss and liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra.
"How is it that this does not become unshakeable? To this he says:
"This is that Meru of poison, the upholder of the earth; one finds no way across its even and uneven places.
Kṛṣṇa says: 'It is difficult to perceive and hard to fathom; who can contemplate it within the mind? (15)

"This is that Meru, difficult to sustain, the upholder of the earth," and so forth. It is "difficult to sustain" (*durdhara*) because the *bodhicitta* is held within it with great difficulty through the six-limbed yoga and the binding of the vital breath (*prāṇabandha*). It is the "upholder of the earth" (*dharaṇidhara*), for it is like Mount Meru itself. In this context, that which flows by way of even conjunctions is "even" (*sama*), the solar flow on the right path; that which flows by way of uneven conjunctions is "uneven" (*viṣama*), the lunar flow on the left path.

With a mind joined to both paths, whether even or uneven, one observes the transformation of the elements of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*). This means that one does not know it in this way. A mind of such a nature does not know that consciousness; it flows by means of the moon and sun as the consciousness-element of beings who are even or uneven. It reaches neither the crossing nor the summit that is so difficult to traverse. For this very reason, he says "Kṛṣṇa," and so forth. Kṛṣṇavajra speaks.

It is difficult to perceive (*durlakṣa*) because it is characterized by the eye of wisdom (*jñānacakṣus*), which is free from the delusion of the state of passion (*virāga*) through suffering; it is so because all things are empty (*sarvaśūnyatva*). It is difficult to fathom (*duravagāha*) because it is experienced as plunging into [the nature of] suffering; for who can contemplate such a reality with the mind?
Who, then, knows that? He says:
He who daily makes the jewel of the mind vibrate with its innate [nature], he alone knows the course of Dharma; what can anyone else know by merely speaking of it? 16.

"Yo saṃveda," and so forth. He who correctly causes [the practitioner] to experience reality as it is through the union of the vajra and lotus and by means of mental support—that which is called "mind" (*manas*) because it reflects upon things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-manana*)—is the jewel that extends *rati*, the unsurpassed bliss; thus it is the "jewel of the mind" (*manoratna*), the image of the Buddha. And so it is said in the *Śrīsamāja*:
"Having established the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, one should not let go of the thought of awakening."
"One should meditate upon the image of the Buddha, which is the entire threefold world without exception.
And likewise in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*:
"The image arises from emptiness; it is the cause, while the result is the bliss born of the immutable."
For this very reason, he says: "Day by day, touching the innate. Day by day, it is as clear as the sky, arising from every [state] that has become empty. And so it is said in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*:
"Born of space, self-existent, the great fire of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*).
Likewise, in the *Śrīsamājottara*:

During the time of service, one should diligently visualize the image as having a great uṣṇīṣa; and during the time of the subsidiary practice (upasādhana), one should visualize the image as Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
"In the *sādhana*, one should visualize the form of the deity and then cause it to be destroyed;
but at the time of the *mahāsādhana*, the mind is the form of the Lord of Buddhas.
This very point is stated regarding the *Kulikā*:

One should stabilize it through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Thus, here is the Lord’s pledge:
Abandoning all thought, one should test it for a single day;
if no conviction arises therein, then my word is false.

In this context, "conviction" (*pratyaya*) refers to the cause, such as smoke and so forth. He who thus experiences the delightful image of the jewel-Buddha in this sequence—"he knows the other"—means he knows the supreme; that is, he realizes the understanding of the nature of phenomena (*dharma*) as it truly is. "What else does he know when it is being told? means that another person, who is attached to the pleasure of the emission of the two organs, what does he think or know? The meaning is that even though it is being explained, he does not understand it.

He states this very point in another way: by virtue of having the wind as its vehicle and consisting of the threefold manifestation, it determines and takes hold of objects through the gateway of the senses, which consist of one hundred and sixty innate dispositions (*prakṛti*).
He who has made the binding of his own mind firm carries away the sixty-one primary dispositions; by him the entire triple world was expanded and then withdrawn again. (17)

"Carrying the path," and so forth. The element of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-dhātu*) carries the path of *saṃsāra*; this refers to the innate body (*sahaja-kāya*) by means of the mind. Binding is the stabilization of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the sixfold yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga-prayoga*), by means of which the obstruction of the moon and sun is achieved. "Having pervaded the entire three worlds"—having pervaded the entire three worlds, consisting of the wheels of body, speech, and mind, up to every single pore of the skin, with the *bodhicitta* through its divisions such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth during the waking state.

Furthermore, by ascending through the dissolution of the fourth state and so forth, according to the divisions of natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) and the rest, [the winds] are withdrawn into the *avadhūtī*. The meaning is that one has directly realized the state of Vajradhara, which transcends sound (*nāda*), drop (*bindu*), and digit (*kalā*), having been introduced into the realm of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyadhātu*).
Therefore he said:
"O Goddess, where can one find the Tathāgata amidst such a multitude of deities? I abide in the moments of the innate nature (sahaja), free from the circle of the mandala. (18)

"Where is the Tathāgata? and so forth. [The question is: "Is the Tathāgata to be found by the hosts of goddesses and wrathful deities? The intention is: "We abide in the moment of the innate (*sahaja*) state, liberated from the maṇḍala-circle. If the deities of the maṇḍala of body, speech, and mind—the aggregates, sense-bases, and so forth—have attained a state of flavor through the instruction on great bliss (*mahāsukha*), then that itself is the Great Maṇḍala; according to this view, there is no other separate maṇḍala. And thus it is said in the *Śrīguhyendutilakatanttra*: "In the *Śrīguhyendratilakatanttra*:
Beyond the cultivation of all limbs, Free from conceptual construction and its products."
This supreme mandala transcends both measure and the bindu.
He speaks again of this very mandala as it was previously described:
"By whom the king of his own mind has been made motionless in the innate state through equal flavor (samarasa), he is perfected at that very moment;
for him there is no longer any fear of old age or death. (19)

"In the innate (*sahaja*), immovable," and so forth. By means of the innate, which is one's own natural wisdom (*prajñā*), that which has been rendered immovable—of an unswerving nature—is the passion of one's own mind, the Vajra-Angara, through the single flavor of the four joys in the state of equal taste (*samarasa*). "He is perfected," and so forth. Perfected means the attainment of Mahāmudrā; he has attained the state of a Vajradhara. "At that very moment" (*tatkṣaṇam*) means by way of many moments.
And it is said in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara* (the *Saṃvarodayatantra*):

"He may, in an instant, become a single embodiment of heaven, earth, and the netherworlds;
yet at that very moment, he is afflicted by one who knows the self-awareness of both himself and others. Thus it is said.
For this very reason, he does not fear old age and death.
Showing the form of Mahāmudrā, he says: "Immovable, free from conceptualization, free from deliberation, devoid of rising and setting, and of excellent essence."
That indeed is called nirvāṇa, wherein the human mind performs no action whatsoever. || 20 ||

"Niścala," and so forth: it is "immovable" because it is infallible; "free from conceptual construction" (*nirvikalpa*) because, having the single flavor of direct experience, it is devoid of the conceptualization that "this is that"; "changeless" (*nirvikāra*) because it has emerged from both passion and dispassion; "devoid of rising and setting" because of the cessation of the sun and the moon; "excellent" (*suṣṭhu śobhana*) because it is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and "essential" (*sāra*) because it is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). "Aïso so," and so forth.

Therefore, *nirvāṇa* is spoken of and designated by the word "nirvāṇa," yet it is not *nirvāṇa* by virtue of having an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), because it is the non-abiding *nirvāṇa* (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*). To explain what that is characterized as, he says: "Wherein the mind of man... and so forth. Wherein, as long as the threefold mind—the hundred and sixty-one fundamental dispositions (*prakṛti*) of the mind—and even the *bindu* (the seminal point) do nothing at all; the meaning is that no such conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*) whatsoever arises.
Therefore he says:
"He who has awakened to the syllable *Evaṃ*, he has awakened to everything without exception.
He becomes a vessel of the Dharma; O friend, wear this garb which belongs to your own Master. (21)

"Evam-kāra," and so forth. That which is such an *evam-kāra* is recognized as the Buddha. The entire universe (*viśva*) is comprised of all *evam-kāras*, because that very [Buddha] is the single form of the universe. What is he like? He says: "He is the casket of the Dharma. This refers to the casket—the locus—of the dharmas, such as the aggregates (*skandhas*), elements (*dhātus*), and sense-bases (*āyatanas*). "Sohu re" is an exclamation. "Wear the attire of your own Lord": this is because he arises only when embraced by the attire—the ornament—of his own Lord, the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*).
Again, he states the summary of the means:
"If a firm lock is placed on the door of the passage of the breath,
and if a jewel-lamp is made in that terrible darkness,"
O Jina-ratna, just as the excellent garment touches the belly, Kṛṣṇa says that even while experiencing worldly existence, one attains liberation. || 22 ||

"Jaï pavaṇagamaṇaduvāra," etc. This refers to the door for the movement of the wind (*pavana*). Then, above that, one performs the firm, indivisible, and unbreakable sealing (*saṃpuṭīkaraṇa*) of the moon and sun, which effects the obstruction of fire; this is what is accomplished, and thus it is called *kāyabandha* (the binding of the body). "Jaï tasu ghorāndhāre": if, in that terrible darkness of the *kumbharūpāsphānaka-samādhi*, the mind is established in the *anāhatanāda*; for the Lord of Dharma (*dharma-īśvara*) himself is the lamp because he is the manifestation of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and he is brought forth or made manifest by means of signs such as smoke and so forth. And so it is said in the *Śrīsamāja*:
"When the mind has entered the vajra of cessation, the grasping of signs arises.

By this, there is the binding of speech. "The jewel of the Jina," and so forth: the "jewel of the Jina" is that very unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*). When, from above, the placement [of the mind] touches the drop (*bindu*) of the sixth gnosis-mandala, he embraces it. And it is said:
"In the sixth vajra-jewel, it resides upon the heads of the Buddhas."
By this, the binding of the mind is accomplished. And so it is said in the Śrīsampuṭa:
"For the sake of satisfying the wind and fire, one should impel [the breath] with the seed-syllable of the Vajrī;
when it is mounted by the *bindu* and *nāda*, it is known as the 'downpour of rain'."
And it is said:
"When [the practitioner] is in every way united with *nāda* and *bindu*, the excellent yogis declare that the fruit is then attained. Thus it is known.

To the question, "What would result from this? he says: "Kṛṣṇa speaks," and so forth. Kṛṣṇavajra says that when existence itself is being experienced—that is, when the bliss of wisdom (*prajñāsukha*) is being directly felt—one attains *nirvāṇa*, the state of Mahāmudrā, because one is liberated from all suffering associated with detachment. Thus, it is said in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*:

"The entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the center; the binding of the movement of the sun and moon in the right and left [channels]; the mind reaching supreme bliss through union with the Mudrā; and the awakening of the Vajra."

The sound of a vajra in the lotus, or the tossing of one's own lotus-like hands for the sake of bliss, the emission of the seed-syllable accompanied by bliss— this is the mouth of the glorious Guru, which removes the fear of death.

Suspecting that everything is accomplished by the binding of the mind alone, he speaks of the immobility of the mind: "He who makes the mind steady here is bound by the noose of the syllables of Dharma; at that very moment, the winds are subdued and the senses become free from desire. (23)

"Whatever is here, motionless," and so forth. One should join [the mind] in the yoga of the vajra-lotus through the application of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and other practices, having rendered the mind motionless. Where? He says: "At the side of the syllable of Dharma. This refers to the unstruck (*anāhata*) syllable, the seed-syllable of Nairātmyā; "at its side" means in that [place]. What would result from this? To this he says: "The wind is bound"—even the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) is bound at that very moment. What else happens? He says: "The poisons become poisonless."
The objects are form and so forth; being enjoyed, they become cast aside. The meaning is that one abandons the bondage of saṃsāra.
Now, as to where the very syllable of Dharma is to be known, he says: "Where the two supreme cessations (paramavirama) are transcended, there one perceives the syllable of Dharma in their midst."
If it were truly so that one could attain perfection by such means, then the wife of the wind would be bound motionless there. || 24 ||

"Supreme and Cessation," and so forth. "Supreme and Cessation" refers to the passion (*rāga*) and the absence of passion (*virāga*) of the moon and the sun. In that regard, observe in the middle. Therein, one should perceive the "syllable of Dharma" (*dharmākṣara*), which possesses the characteristics previously described, situated between those two. "Aïsa uesa," and so forth. If all this is clearly accomplished and perfected through such instruction on the Way of Mantra (*mantranaya*), then the "consort of the wind" (*pavanagṛhiṇī*), possessing the aforementioned characteristics, is certainly bound; that is to say, she becomes motionless.

Now, when this bond of the vital breath has become motionless, one might ask: what is the form of the imperishable syllable of Dharma, the Mahāsukha-vajra, and where does it dwell? To this he says: “The excellent jewel on the peak of the mountain is lofty; there the Sage dwells in solitude. He cannot be overstepped even by lions, nor can the noble elephant reach his hope. (25)

"Upon the peak of the mountain of excellent jewels," and so forth. The "mountain of excellent jewels" is that very Meru mentioned previously. Its "peak" or summit is the form of bliss in the lotus-abode (*kamalabhavana*), because it is the support of all great bliss. It is the "supreme limb," the great plateau. Regarding the phrase "where the Lord made His dwelling": it means where the Blessed One—the "Lord" (*savara*) consisting of the imperishable reality (*akṣara*) attained in such a manner, who is the diamond of gnosis (*jñānavajra*)—has made His abode. To describe His specific qualities, he says: "That [place] cannot be transgressed," and so forth.

She has crossed over nine [oceans] which are occupied by lions with five-fold circular faces, because the sixth is of the nature of the *jñānamaṇḍala*. "She has leaped far beyond the best of elephants" (*karivara*): the "best of elephants" refers to a beast; she has leaped far beyond both the moon and the sun. And it is said: "The moon and the sun are great beasts. This is the intended meaning.

Although the Blessed One, Mahāsukha-Vajra, abides everywhere, at all times, and in every way as the element of consciousness mounted upon the wind that carries the orbs of the moon and sun, he is not realized. This is because the ground of the elephant-king of the mind—the "elephant" (karivara)—is [attained] by the lion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which consists of the five orbs.
Nevertheless, he states where one dwells by necessity within the body born of karma:
"This is that best of mountains described by me; this is that state of great bliss.
Only one night—a moment of the innate—is obtained, as long as the great bliss [endures]. (26)

"This is that best of mountains," and so forth. The meaning is: this very best of mountains has been described by me, Kṛṣṇavajra, and not by anyone else; those like me are capable of describing it. "This indeed is the place of great bliss" (*ehu so mahāsuhaṭhāva*); by way of exposition, this very place of great bliss is the aforementioned plateau. "This indeed is the innate joy," and so forth. Right here, one should practice that innate moment (*sahajakṣaṇa*) until reaching the state of Vajradhara. For this very reason, "great bliss is obtained" (*labbhaï mahāsuha*), as far as the station of Vajradhara, the Lord of the Thirteenth Bhūmi, is attained.
Anticipating the question, "In what state does this Vajradhara abide? [the author] says:
"Having merged with the body, speech, and mind of all beings, he flashes forth everywhere, even at a distance."
Thus, upon the dissolution of discursive thought, there is but one great bliss, nirvana. 27.

"Entire world," and so forth. All those Tathāgatas, such as Vairocana and the others, take the form of the world through the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) beginning with form. Their consorts, Locanā and the others, consist of the elements (*dhātu*) such as earth and the rest, which are the body, speech, and mind of those [Tathāgatas]. They are united with them; the meaning is that the body of Vajradhara—characterized by the glory of the perfect awakening of great passion (*mahārāga*) in which [all] have become a single, unified mass—is, according to the analogy of water and milk, of one flavor (*samarasa*) with these.

"Viphuraï" (it flashes forth): therein, within that very body of Vajradhara, that same [body, speech, mind, etc. flashes forth according to the analogy of waves upon water. By this, it is meant that the triple world is the vajra-body, and so forth. Clarifying this very point, he says: "So vitakka" (that conceptualization), etc. Each individual Great Bliss King, Vajradhara, manifests in various ways.
Regarding where he dwells by way of bodily constraint, he says:
"He performs no mantra nor tantra,
but is sporting with his own wife."
As long as the mistress of the house does not bathe in her own home, how can one wander about adorned with the five colors? || 28 ||

"Not even one [is performed]—no mantra, etc. Not even a single mantra, tantra, recitation (*japa*), or tantric reading is performed. To the question "By whom?", he says: "In their own home," and so forth. Their own wife is the *jñānamudrā*, appearing as one's own mind; having taken her through the instruction of a true guru, yogins perform the play of the innate (*sahaja*) with a consort who is pleasing to the mind. And thus it is said in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*:
"The mere appearance of the mind, produced within one's own mind like a reflection in a mirror, is to be cultivated by the lords of yogins and served by all the sons of the Victors and the Buddhas."
"That flame of gnosis, once awakened, burns away the entire host of Māras along with their objects;
through the yoga of the rain, it also burns away passion and the like within the body, bestowing equal bliss upon yogins.

Thus it is said. For a yogin who is attached to this Blessed Lady, there is no need to grasp at mantras or tantras. This is its meaning: she alone is the *mantra*, because she is the mentalizing (*manana*) of the mind, which is the *bodhicitta*; and she alone is the "holding of the vessel" (*tattrikumbhadhāraṇa*).
Because of the recitation of the *dhātupāṭha*, everything is indeed performed by one who is then attached to that [practice] while holding the *jinakumbha*. And so it is said in the *Śrīsamāja*:
"There is no mantra-recitation, no austerity, and no fire-offering."
Neither the mandala-dweller nor the mandala itself;
that is the recitation of mantra, that is austerity, that is the fire offering—that is the mandala-dweller and that is the mandala. Thus it is said.

"Indeed, in one's own house" means that one's own house is the abode of *avadhūtī*, which is the emptiness of all things (*sarvaśūnyatā*). She alone, who has taken up the consort of the *mahāmudrā* tantra, neither sinks nor dissolves. To that extent, what is the use of the five colors and so forth? That is to say, what is the use of the five colors, the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*), or these various arms, faces, colors, and forms, which are designated according to the diverse dispositions of many sentient beings? And thus it is said in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*: "Through union with the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), through reliance on the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*), and through the singular yoga of the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), that imperishable [state] attains increase."
Then:
Having hands and feet everywhere, having eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
possessing memory everywhere in the world, He stands encompassing all.
One should demonstrate, according to the rule, the instructional points for accomplishing the fruit of Mahāmudrā through that very same Divine Mudrā.
He says that very thing again:
"Day after day you remain engaged in performing these dharmas of recitation, fire-oblation, and mandala-rites."
Without constant love for the young woman, how can enlightenment be attained even with this very body? || 29 ||

"These [practices of] recitation, fire-offering," and so forth. By this, the meaning is that you remain day after day with your mind bound externally through external fire-offerings, recitation, and mandala rituals, in the form of a practitioner, yet you are fruitless. To explain how all of this is fruitless, he says: "Without him," and so forth. Without him, because she is always composed of passion (*rāga*), she alone is the divine consort (*divyamudrā*).

The arising [of enlightenment] occurs through passion, delimited by her continuous movement, in the sequence beginning with bliss; by that affection—that waveless affection of a young woman—[it is attained]. "What is obtained? and so forth: *bodhi* is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*); what is that obtained by him? The meaning is that the aforementioned syllable *Evaṃ* is not obtained without the body.
That rare moment of the innate nature which was realized by whom?
By that, O world, all these various conceptualizations of poison have been shattered; indeed, everything is of a limited measure.
"Since he has taken his own wife here, having made the jewel of his mind utterly steady—O friend, such is the meaning of the word 'vājira' (horse); this is the ultimate truth. 31.

"That which was awakened," and so forth, is easy to understand. "That which was made immovable," and so forth: by whom was the jewel of the mind—the *bodhicitta*—made immovable because it cannot be moved after having melted the fire of the fierce *caṇḍālī*? To answer "having done what," he says: "Having taken his own wife," and so forth; that very one's own wife, who is the divine *mudrā*, in that place of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) known as the syllable *vaṃ*. "He is indeed that Vajra-holder," and so forth: he is the Lord Vajradhara, the master of body, speech, and mind. "O, the syllable of perfect awakening! (*re sambodhākṣaram*).
"Paramārtha has been spoken": this means that the uncontrived ultimate reality (paramārtha) has been stated by me, Kṛṣṇavajra; the meaning is that there is nothing else here.
He gives this very example: "Just as salt dissolves in water, so does the mind when taken by a wife;
it becomes of equal flavor at that moment, provided it is again united with them. (32)

"Just as salt dissolves," and so forth. Just as salt dissolves in water, so too, having taken hold of the housewife who is the embodiment of gnosis (*jñāna*), the mind—that is, the *bodhicitta*—attains a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*). And thus it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"The Blessed One takes the form of semen; that bliss is the bliss of the beloved.

Both of these—the semen and the bliss—are of the nature of the support and the supported within the bliss whose intrinsic nature is the universal void (*sarvaśūnya*). They attain a state of equal flavor, a single state of integration, at that very moment.
And so it is said in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*:

"The relationship between the support and the supported persists as long as the state of immutability (*akṣaratā*) has not been reached. Once the mind has attained immutability, it no longer possesses the characteristics of support and supported."
And so it is stated in the *Saṃpuṭa*:
"That which comes through the two apertures of the nostrils is called 'good time' (*sukāla*); that which goes out is indeed 'bad time' (*duṣkāla*). One of these two is thus proclaimed."
One should be alone and without companion; time has become inconceivable.
Devoid of breath control (prāṇāyāma), it is characterized by exhalation and inhalation.
Free from coming and going, it is called the single *samaya*;
there is neither passion nor dispassion, and the middle is not perceived.
"By means of both passion and dispassion, the Unstruck (anāhata) [sound] sets;
just as clarified butter poured into clarified butter becomes mixed and undisturbed, so too, through passion and dispassion, there is a single state of equal flavor. Thus it is said.

"Where again is their permanence? means: if, moreover, permanence were delimited by those two [mutually], then this would be the case. This is the meaning: through the aforementioned methods, the semen and the blood (rajas), which consist of the nature of the moon and the sun, are not mutually delimited; provided that they are not distinct. The nature of the semen is the Moon-nature, the Sambhogakāya; and the nature of the blood is the Sun-illumination, the Nirmāṇakāya. [This occurs] when [dualistic perception] has set, together with the consort who holds the form of the wick of bliss.

This *bodhicitta*, having become condensed through both yogas and having transcended the path of saṃsāra characterized by the forms of arising and dissolution, becomes of equal flavor (*samarasībhavati*) and manifests as the natural outflow (*niṣyanda-rūpa*) of Śrī Heruka. Thus it is said in the *Sampuṭa*:
"When the moon is situated in the throat in the form of great passion (*mahārāga*), that is declared to be the supreme body of the Buddhas, the *saṃbhoga*."
When he is always situated at the tip of the nose, which is the tip of the vajra,
then the sambhogakāya indeed becomes set at rest.
Having entered into the center of the bhaga, he is renowned as the mustard seed;
designated as the form of the sun, he is called the nirmāṇakāya.
Through that, there arises the pervasive manifestation of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
he is known as the King Padmanarteśvara, the Lord of the Lotus Light. Thus it is said.
The commentary on the *Dohākoṣa* of Śrī Kṛṣṇavajrapāda is completed.
This is the work of the scholar Amṛtavajra. The extent of the text is four hundred [verses]. May it be auspicious! It was written by Śrīrūparāja for the purpose of his own spiritual awakening.
